newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - WALL STREET JOURNAL - SEPT 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - WALL STREET JOURNAL - SEPT 23.

text.p: The seven regional "baby bells" are nearing the sale of their jointly owned research operations to Science Applications International Corp (SAIC), for $700 million.
* AT&T Corp Chairman Robert Allen completed a short list for a new president and has told directors at the company that he plans to step down early.
* KPMG Peat Marwick is expected to name Stephen Butler chairman and chief executive.
* Microsoft Corp is delaying plans to run classified ads in planned online information guides, an idea that had implications for the newspaper industry.
* Merrill Lynch and Co Inc is considering offering to investors its own stock-index funds.
* General Motors Corp will cut in half the amount holders of its gold credit card can earn toward the purchase of a new car or truck.
* The U.S. Department of Justice is still investigating Citibank's handling of more than $100 million for Raul Salinas, the brother of Mexico's former president.
* The Federal Bureau of Investigation is looking for Calvin Grigsby, the missing former head of the bond firm Grigsby Branford, to learn how the firm obtained a $183 million muni-bond deal.
* Archer Daniels Midland filed a $30 million lawsuit against former executive Mark Whitacre.
* The Sulzberger family took actions to reassert control of the New York Times Co after Lance Primis, a family outsider, resigned as president.
* ~Coopers & Lybrand~agreed to pay the government $2.3 million to avoid charges stemming from dealings with indicted Arizona Gov. J. Fife Symington.
* America Online Inc received court permission to resume blocking junk e-mail.
* J.B. Hunt's plan to give its drivers pay raises of an average 33 percent could have sweeping consequences for the economy if it raises shipping costs also.
* Coca-Cola told analysts its global volume in the third quarter will rise six percent to seven percent, below analysts' estimates.
* Whether Warren Buffet has been right or wrong about a stock, investors don't like to see him get out if they're still in. - Heard on the Street.
